title: Level 8 · Coding Logic and Problem Solving
blurb: Classic interview-style problems: numbers, patterns, strings, searching, sorting and core data structures and techniques.

lessons.title: Number Programs
lessons.concept: Many classic problems are about digits and divisors. A number is prime if only 1 and itself divide it evenly, so you test divisors with % (remainder). For 7, try 2, 3, 4, 5, 6: none give remainder 0, so 7 is prime. For 9, 9 % 3 == 0, so it is not. Other classics: a palindrome number reads the same backwards (121) and an Armstrong number equals the sum of its digits each raised to the number of digits (153 = 1 + 125 + 27).
lessons.why: Divisor checks and digit tricks appear in validation (check digits on cards), cryptography and every coding interview.
lessons.example:
n = 153
digits = str(n)
total = sum(int(d) ** len(digits) for d in digits)
print(total == n)
print(str(121) == str(121)[::-1])
lessons.example_note: Shows that 153 is an Armstrong number and 121 is a palindrome.

lessons.title: Pattern Programs
lessons.concept: Patterns are drawn with nested loops: the outer loop picks the row, the inner part decides what goes on that row. A star triangle of 3 rows prints *, then **, then ***: row i has i stars, so print('*' * i) inside for i in range(1, 4) does it. Number patterns work the same way, only you build the row from numbers.
lessons.why: Patterns train you to think about rows and columns, which is the heart of tables, grids, game boards and text reports.
lessons.prompt: Read an integer n from input. Print a number triangle with n rows where row i shows the numbers 1 to i separated by spaces. For 3 it prints 1, 1 2, 1 2 3 on three lines.
lessons.starter:
n = int(input())
# for each row i from 1 to n, print the numbers 1..i separated by spaces
hints: Use an outer loop for i in range(1, n + 1).
For each row, build the numbers 1..i. You can use a second loop or ' '.join(...) with str().
print(' '.join(str(j) for j in range(1, i + 1)))

lessons.title: String Problems
lessons.concept: Strings can be sliced and looped over like lists. text[::-1] reverses a string, and a palindrome equals its own reverse. Two words are anagrams when they use exactly the same letters: 'listen' and 'silent' both sort to 'eilnst'. So to compare anagrams, clean both words (lowercase, no spaces) and compare their sorted letters.
lessons.why: Text cleaning and comparison power search boxes, spell checkers, duplicate detection and word games.
lessons.example:
word = 'Level'
clean = word.lower()
print(clean == clean[::-1])
print(sorted('listen') == sorted('silent'))
lessons.example_note: Checks a palindrome and an anagram pair.

lessons.title: Array/List Problems
lessons.concept: Most list problems are one pass: walk through the items and keep a few tracking variables. To find the largest, start with the first item as best and replace it whenever you meet something bigger. To find duplicates, remember what you have seen; if an item is already in seen, it is a duplicate.
lessons.why: Finding highest scores, lowest prices and repeated entries is everyday data work.

Loop over nums, updating them with if x > largest / if x < smallest.
Keep a set called seen; if x is already in it, add x to another set of duplicates. Return sorted(dups).

lessons.title: Searching
lessons.concept: Linear search checks items one by one until it finds the target: simple, works on any list. Binary search needs a sorted list: look at the middle item; if the target is smaller, keep only the left half, otherwise the right half, and repeat. Searching 1,000,000 items takes about 20 steps instead of 1,000,000.
lessons.why: Dictionaries, databases and phone contact lists use halving ideas to find things fast.

If nums[mid] is smaller than target, set low = mid + 1; if bigger, set high = mid - 1.
If nums[mid] == target, return mid. After the loop ends, return -1.

lessons.title: Sorting
lessons.concept: Sorting puts items in order. Bubble sort repeatedly swaps neighbours that are in the wrong order. Selection sort picks the smallest remaining item and puts it next. Insertion sort takes each item and slides it left into its place, like arranging playing cards in your hand. Merge sort and quick sort split the list, sort the parts and combine them, which is much faster for big lists. Example: insertion sort on [3, 1, 2] gives [1, 3, 2], then [1, 2, 3].
lessons.why: Sorted data is easier to search, compare and display, from leaderboards to bank statements.
lessons.example:
nums = [4, 2, 5, 1]
for i in range(1, len(nums)):
    key = nums[i]
    j = i - 1
    while j >= 0 and nums[j] > key:
        nums[j + 1] = nums[j]
        j -= 1
    nums[j + 1] = key
print(nums)

lessons.title: Two Pointers
lessons.concept: The two pointers trick uses two index variables that move towards each other (or in the same direction) so one pass is enough. To find two numbers in a sorted list that add to 9, put left at the start and right at the end. If the sum is too small move left up, if too big move right down. Reversing an array uses the same pointers: swap the ends, then move both inwards.
lessons.why: It turns slow 'check every pair' code into fast one-pass code, used in matching, merging and cleaning data.
lessons.example_note: Finds the pair 2 and 7 that adds to 9.

lessons.title: Sliding Window
lessons.concept: A sliding window is a fixed-size block that moves along a list one step at a time. Instead of re-adding every window from scratch, you add the new item that enters and subtract the item that leaves. For [2, 1, 5, 1] with k = 2: windows are 2+1=3, then 3+5-2=6, then 6+1-1=6.
lessons.why: Moving averages, rate limits and 'best 7 days of sales' all use sliding windows.
lessons.example:
nums = [2, 1, 5, 1]
k = 2
window = sum(nums[:k])
print(window)
for i in range(k, len(nums)):
    window += nums[i] - nums[i - k]
    print(window)
lessons.prompt: Write max_window_sum(nums, k) that returns the largest sum of any k neighbouring numbers. If k is bigger than the list, return 0. Slide the window instead of re-adding it each time.
hints: Start with window = sum(nums[:k]) and best = window.
Loop i from k to len(nums) - 1: window += nums[i] - nums[i - k].
After each slide, update best if window is larger. Return best.

lessons.title: Hashing
lessons.concept: A hash table (a Python dict) finds a key almost instantly, no matter how big it is. A classic use is frequency counting: loop over the items and do counts[x] = counts.get(x, 0) + 1. For 'a b a' the counts become a: 2, b: 1. The same idea finds duplicates: any key whose count is above 1 is repeated.
lessons.why: Word counts, vote tallies, inventory totals and 'have I seen this user?' checks all use hashing.
lessons.example_note: Counts words and prints them in alphabetical order.
lessons.prompt: Write word_counts(text) that lowercases the text, splits it into words and returns a sorted list of (word, count) tuples. For an empty text return an empty list.
hints: text.lower().split() gives the list of words.
counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1 adds one to the count.
Finish with return sorted(counts.items()).

lessons.title: Stack
lessons.concept: A stack is last in, first out, like a pile of plates: you append to the top and pop from the top. To check balanced brackets, push every opening bracket; when you see a closing one, the top of the stack must be its matching opener. For '(]' the ']' arrives but the top is '(', so it is not balanced. At the end the stack must be empty.
lessons.why: Undo buttons, browser back history and code editors checking your brackets all use stacks.
lessons.example_note: Pushes two brackets, then pops the most recent one.
lessons.prompt: Write is_balanced(s) that returns True if every ( [ { in s is closed in the correct order, otherwise False. An empty string is balanced. Use a list as a stack with append and pop.
hints: Push opening brackets with stack.append(ch).
For a closing bracket, fail if the stack is empty or stack.pop() is not the matching opener.
At the end return len(stack) == 0.

lessons.title: Queue
lessons.concept: A queue is first in, first out, like people waiting at a ticket counter: the one who joined first is served first. You enqueue at the back and dequeue from the front. A plain list is slow at removing from the front, so Python gives collections.deque with fast append and popleft.
lessons.why: Print jobs, customer support tickets and message systems all line work up in queues.
lessons.example:
from collections import deque
q = deque()
q.append('Asha')
q.append('Ravi')
print(q.popleft())
print(len(q))
lessons.example_note: Asha joined first so she leaves first.
lessons.prompt: Complete the class Queue using a deque inside. Methods: enqueue(x) adds to the back, dequeue() removes and returns the front item (or None if empty), size() gives the count, is_empty() gives True/False.
hints: Every method takes self as its first parameter.
enqueue uses self.items.append(x); dequeue uses self.items.popleft().
Check if not self.items before popleft, since popping an empty deque raises an error.

cases.expr: (lambda q: (q.enqueue(1), q.enqueue(2), q.enqueue(3), q.dequeue(), q.dequeue(), q.dequeue(), q.dequeue(), q.is_empty()))(Queue())

lessons.title: Linked List
lessons.concept: A linked list is a chain of Node objects. Each node holds a value and a next link to the following node; the last one has next = None. To reverse a list, walk along it with three names: prev (starts None), cur (the head) and a saved nxt. At each node point cur.next back at prev, then step forward. To detect a cycle, move a slow and a fast pointer; if they ever meet, the chain loops.
lessons.why: Linked chains are behind music playlists, browser history and the way many languages manage memory.
lessons.example:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, value):
        self.value = value
        self.next = None

a = Node(1)
b = Node(2)
a.next = b
cur = a
while cur:
    print(cur.value)
    cur = cur.next
lessons.example_note: Links two nodes and walks along them, printing 1 then 2.
lessons.prompt: The Node class and helpers build(values) and to_list(head) are given. Write reverse_list(head) that reverses the chain and returns the new head. Use the prev/cur idea.
hints: Inside the loop first save nxt = cur.next so you do not lose the rest.
Then cur.next = prev, prev = cur, cur = nxt.
When the loop ends prev is the new head, so return prev.

lessons.title: Trees
lessons.concept: A binary tree is made of nodes that each have a left and a right child. In a binary search tree (BST) smaller values go left and bigger values go right. To insert 4 into a tree with root 5, go left (4 is less than 5) and place it there. Reading the tree in-order (left, node, right) gives the values in sorted order. Both steps are naturally recursive: do the same job on the left or right child.
lessons.why: Trees organise file folders, web page structure (HTML) and database indexes.
lessons.example:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, value):
        self.value = value
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

root = Node(5)
root.left = Node(3)
root.right = Node(8)
def inorder(n):
    return inorder(n.left) + [n.value] + inorder(n.right) if n else []
print(inorder(root))
lessons.prompt: The Node class and build_bst(values) (which calls your insert for each value) are given. Write insert(root, value) that adds a value to the BST and returns the root (ignore duplicates), and inorder(root) that returns the sorted list of values. An empty tree gives [].
hints: Base case: if root is None, return Node(value) for insert and [] for inorder.
insert: when value < root.value set root.left = insert(root.left, value); when bigger do the same on the right.
inorder returns inorder(root.left) + [root.value] + inorder(root.right). Insert must return root.

lessons.title: Graphs
lessons.concept: A graph is dots (nodes) joined by lines (edges), stored as an adjacency dict such as {'A': ['B', 'C'], 'B': [], 'C': []} meaning A connects to B and C. BFS (breadth-first search) explores level by level using a queue: visit A, then B and C, then their neighbours. DFS (depth-first search) goes as deep as possible first using a stack or recursion. Always remember which nodes you have visited so loops do not run forever.
lessons.why: Maps and route finding, social networks ('friends of friends') and web crawlers are all graph problems.

lessons.title: Recursion
lessons.concept: Recursion means a function calls itself on a smaller version of the problem, with a base case that stops it. To list all subsets of [1, 2]: take the subsets of the rest [2], which are [] and [2], then also add 1 to each. That gives [], [2], [1], [1, 2]. Permutations work similarly: pick each item as the first one and arrange the rest.
lessons.why: Folder trees, nested menus, puzzles and many search problems are solved most naturally with recursion.
lessons.example_note: Adds 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 0 using a function that calls itself.

lessons.title: Backtracking
lessons.concept: Backtracking builds an answer one choice at a time. If a choice breaks a rule, you undo it (step back) and try the next one. In the N-Queens puzzle you place one queen per row; for each column check that no earlier queen shares the column or a diagonal. If a row has no safe column, go back and move the previous queen. Two queens on diagonal share row - col or row + col.
lessons.why: Sudoku solvers, maze finders and scheduling tools all try a choice, test it and undo it if it fails.
lessons.example_note: Counts the 2 ways to place 4 queens safely on a 4x4 board.

lessons.title: Dynamic Programming
lessons.concept: Dynamic programming solves a big problem by solving small overlapping pieces once and remembering the answers (memoization). Fibonacci is the classic: fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2), and caching stops it recomputing the same values millions of times. Climbing stairs (1 or 2 steps at a time) has the same shape: ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2). The knapsack problem uses the same idea: remember the best value for each capacity.
lessons.why: Route planning, spell correction, text diffing and budgeting problems rely on dynamic programming.
